Accurate modeling of these devices is essential not only to predict performance but also to address real-time control challenges, including dynamic response to load changes and fault conditions (Zhu et al. 2020). Generic physics-based inverter models often rely on detailed SPICE simulations or control-theoretic equations to capture converter behavior under nominal conditions (Iero et al. 2014; Bennai et al. 2024). While such approaches can be precise, they require comprehensive knowledge of component parameters and are computationally intensive, making them impractical for large-scale system studies or real-time applications. Furthermore, these models may struggle to account for nonlinearities arising from parasitic elements and changing environmental factors such as irradiance or temperature (W. Li et al. 2021). To overcome these limitations, recent research has turned to data-driven, machine learning (ML) techniques that learn the inverter’s input-output mapping directly from experimental measurements (Guruwacharya et al. 2024). Neural architectures—ranging from recurrent networks like Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) to convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and attention-based Transformers—have shown strong capabilities in capturing complex, time-dependent dynamics without explicit physical equations (Shiri et al. 2023; Buestán-Andrade et al. 2023). For instance, LSTM and GRU models excel at modeling long-term dependencies in voltage and current time series, while CNNs efficiently extract local waveform features, and Transformers leverage self-attention for global temporal patterns (Saffari and Khodayar 2024). Empirical studies confirm the promise of ML-based inverter modeling. Fan et al. (Fan et al. 2022) demonstrated that neural networks trained on power-hardware-in-the-loop data can closely match commercial microinverter dynamics in the frequency domain (Kaufhold et al. 2021; Guruwacharya et al. 2022). Similarly, data-driven impedance model- ing has accurately reproduced converter response across operating points, addressing issues such as grid impedance variation and control interactions (Y. Li et al. 2024). These methods not only improve predictive accuracy but also adapt automatically to different operating conditions and component aging. Building on this foundation, our work evaluates multiple ML architectures — LSTM (Hochreiter 1998), GRU (Chung et al. 2014), CNN (O’Shea and Nash 2015), and Transformer (Vaswani et al. 2017) — on experimental data collected from commercial three-phase inverters under varied DC power input, voltage, and frequency conditions. We compare these models’ accuracy, training time, and inference time, highlighting trade-offs between complexity and performance in inverter modeling. The remainder of the technical report is organized as follows. In Section 2, we describe the inverter testbed and data- acquisition methodology, detailing the voltage-sweep and frequency-sweep experiments conducted to generate the modeling dataset. Section 3 presents the ML models used for inverter prediction, their implemented architecture, and performance results.
